topic_lead: Against fate and fixed natures, the early fathers insist that human beings can choose — or the language of reward, blame, counsel, and judgment collapses. Voices range from the well-known apologists to Methodius, Hermas, and Lactantius.
author: Justin Martyr
english: But so that no one, from what we said earlier, will think we claim that events happen by the necessity of fate — just because they were foretold as things known in advance — we will clear this up too.
We have learned through the prophets, and we declare it true, that punishments, chastisements, and good repayments are given according to the worth of each person’s deeds.

If that were not so, and everything instead happened by fate, then nothing at all would be in our power. For if it is fated that this one be good and that one worthless, then the first is not to be approved and the second not to be blamed.
And again: unless the human race has power, by free deliberate choice, to flee what is shameful and to choose what is fine, it is not accountable for whatever is done.

But that it both succeeds and fails by free deliberate choice, we prove as follows. We see the same human being turning to pursue opposite things. If it had been fated that he be either worthless or excellent, he would never have been able to receive both opposites, nor change so often.

Nor would some be excellent and others worthless — for then we would make fate the cause of both good and worthless things, acting against itself — or else that earlier claim would seem true: that there is no virtue and no vice, only opinion labeling things good or bad, which, as the true Word shows, is the greatest impiety and injustice.
But we say this is unbreakable ‘fate’: that those who choose what is fine receive fitting rewards, and those who likewise choose the opposite receive fitting wages.

For God did not make the human being like other things — trees and four-footed animals — that can do nothing by choice. He would not deserve reward or praise if he did not choose the good from himself, but were simply made that way; nor, if he were bad, would he justly meet with punishment, not being such from himself, but unable to be anything other than what he had been made.
translator_notes: Source-locked to First1KGreek Justin 1 Apology 43. See justification receipt for προαίρεσις ἐλευθέρα and fate vocabulary.

author: Justin Martyr
english: We are persuaded that each person will receive according to his deeds at the judgment of God. That conviction keeps us from wrongdoing, and it draws us toward a life that can stand in his sight.

author: Justin Martyr
english: As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and who undertake to live accordingly, are taught to pray and ask God with fasting for the forgiveness of their past sins — and we pray and fast with them.

Then they are brought by us to where there is water, and they are reborn in the same way we ourselves were reborn. In the name of God the Father and Master of all, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they receive the washing with water.
translator_notes: Baptism tied to persuaded faith and a willing new way of life — not bare coercion.

author: Tatian
english: Evil does not have the nature of the good — that nature belongs to God alone. Among human beings it is completed by the freedom of deliberate choice, so that the worthless person is justly punished, having become wicked through himself, and the just person is worthily praised for noble deeds, not having transgressed God's will by the self-determining power given from God.
translator_notes: Source-locked Tatian Oratio ad Graecos Greek. Replaces shorter ANF-mediated draft.

author: Athenagoras
english: Virtue belongs to those who can choose the good. There is no virtue in what cannot turn either way. The stars keep their courses by necessity; we are praised or blamed because we move ourselves.
translator_notes: Philosophical Athenian tone — keep the cool precision.

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: If he turns instead to the works of death, disobeying God, he himself is the cause of his own death. For God made the human being free and self-determining.
What he procured for himself through carelessness and disobedience, God now gives him through his own kindness and mercy — when the human being obeys him.
Just as by disobeying, the human being drew death on himself, so by obeying the will of God, the one who wants to can procure eternal life for himself. For God gave us a law and holy commandments.
translator_notes: Source-locked Theophilus Ad Autolycum Greek (First1K/Perseus).

author: Irenaeus
english: That saying of the Lord — How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were not willing — sets out the ancient law of human liberty. From the beginning God made man free, possessing his own power, so that he might obey God willingly and not by force.

There is no coercion with God. A good will toward us is always present with him. Therefore he gives good counsel to all. In human beings, as in angels, he placed the power of choice, so that those who obeyed might justly possess the good — given by God, yet kept by themselves.
translator_notes: Pastoral-polemical weight; keep Scripture woven in.

added_allusions.reason: How often I wanted… you would not.

author: Irenaeus
english: Not only in works but also in faith has God kept the will of man free and under his own control. According to your faith be it done to you — showing that faith belongs to the person who believes.

All things are possible to the one who believes. Go; as you have believed, so let it be done for you. Such words show that a human being is in his own power with respect to faith. The one who believes in him has eternal life; the one who does not believe the Son does not have eternal life.

added_allusions.reason: All things possible to him who believes.
Believes / does not believe the Son.

author: Irenaeus
english: If you are the work of God, wait for the hand of your Maker who does everything at the right time. Present him a soft and willing heart, and keep the form in which the Craftsman shaped you. Soften the clay in yourself, lest by hardening you lose his fingerprints.

By keeping the structure you will ascend to what is perfect. God’s craftsmanship hides the moisture of clay within you. His hand formed your substance. He will cover you inside and out with pure gold and silver, and he will adorn you so that the King himself may delight in your beauty.
translator_notes: Cooperation image: willing clay, not coerced stone — preserve the metaphor.

author: Irenaeus
english: The Lord has redeemed us by his own blood and given his soul for our souls and his flesh for our flesh. He has poured out the Spirit of the Father to bring about the union and communion of God and humankind.
Bringing God down to human beings through the Spirit, and lifting humanity to God through his incarnation, he truly and surely bestowed on us immortality by communion with God.

author: Irenaeus
english: He has therefore summed up all things in himself: the war against our enemy, and the crushing of the one who led us captive in Adam. The enemy would not have been justly conquered unless it were a man who conquered him.

For at first it was through a man that the enemy gained power over us and held us — a man who was not yet under his power. In the same way, the enemy was overcome by a man, and we who had been conquered were set free.
translator_notes: Recapitulation / Christus Victor tone — keep Adam–Christ symmetry.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Neither praise nor blame, neither rewards nor punishments, would be just if the soul did not have the power of choosing and refusing, and if evil were involuntary.
translator_notes: Teacherly Alexandrian compression.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Being baptized, we are illuminated; being illuminated, we become sons; being made sons, we are made perfect; being made perfect, we are made immortal. I, he says, have said, You are gods and all sons of the Most High.

added_allusions.reason: You are gods… sons of the Most High.

author: Tertullian
english: I find that man was constituted free by God — master of his own will and of his own power. Nothing shows God’s goodness more clearly than this gift: liberty of the will.

God alone is good by nature. Man has a beginning; he is not good by nature in the same way, but by creation he is pointed toward the good. So that he might have a goodness of his own, God set freedom in him — freedom either for obedience or for resistance.
If man were good or evil by necessity and not by choice, there would be no room for reward or punishment. Take away choice, and you take away the whole case.
translator_notes: Keep Tertullian’s forensic bite; do not pious-wash.

author: Tertullian
english: Repentance is life, because it is preferred to death. You who were once far off are invited near — not by force, but by the summons of a goodness that would rather restore than destroy.
translator_notes: Short excerpt; full chapter upgrade queued.

author: Hippolytus
english: This is the God who was preached by the law and the prophets, and whom the new covenant of grace has now made known. This is the Word who became man for our sake, so that through him we might attain the standing of children.
translator_notes: Lesser-read in topical tools; include for breadth.

author: Origen
english: There are certain movements in animals that come from themselves, and others that come from outside. Rational beings have, in addition, reason — the judge of how they should move.

It is ours either to use our natural movements toward what is good, or to turn them toward the opposite. We are not compelled like a stone falling downward, nor like a plant that only grows as its nature allows.
translator_notes: Preserve Origen’s exploratory, layered tone; hedges matter.

author: Origen
english: It is not as if we receive nothing from God when we act. The good we do is not accomplished without God — yet it is not accomplished without us either. Scripture shows both: that it depends on us, and that the end is from God.

author: Origen
english: God does not leave the world without a call. The word goes out; some receive it, some refuse. The refusal does not prove the call was never given.
translator_notes: Compressed paraphrase of Origen’s anti-determinist apologetic line; expand on Greek pass.

author: Methodius of Olympus
english: Orthodox: I do not think it right to say that human beings were made by God as mere necessities. I say the first human was made self-determining — that is, free — and from him the heirs of the race inherited the same freedom.

So I affirm that the human being was made free, yet a slave to whatever he wills to serve. I say this is the greatest gift given him by God. For all other things serve the divine command by necessity: if you speak of heaven, it stands bearing its Master, not leaving its appointed place; if of the sun, it completes its set course, not refusing the run, but serving the Master by a kind of necessity.

Earth likewise you see fixed and bearing the command of the one who ordered it. The rest also serve the Maker by necessity, none of them able to do anything other than that for which it was made. Therefore we do not praise them for obeying the Master this way, nor is a better hope laid up for them, because they kept the command unwillingly.

But the human being received authority to obey whatever he wills, bringing himself into service — not mastered by necessity of nature, nor stripped of power. I say this was granted for the sake of better things, so that he might receive something more than he has from the Better One — something that comes to him from obedience and that he may claim from his Maker as what is due.
translator_notes: Source-locked Methodius De Libero Arbitrio (First1KGreek). Dialogue speaker: Orthodox.

author: Novatian
english: The rule of truth requires that we believe first in God the Father and Almighty Lord — and in the Son of God, Christ Jesus, the Lord our God, but the Son of God, that is, of that God who is both one and true — through whom we have been restored and made alive.
translator_notes: Often skipped; include for Roman third-century breadth.

citation: Cyprian — On the Unity of the Church 6
author: Cyprian
work: On the Unity of the Church
english: He cannot have God for his Father who does not have the Church for his mother. If anyone could escape outside Noah’s ark, then someone outside the Church might escape as well.
translator_notes: Ecclesiological soteriology — keep the hard edge; label development as debate for later readers.

author: Lactantius
english: God gave wisdom to the human race for this reason above all: that we might know our Maker, and that we might pursue virtue, which alone can lead us to immortality.
Virtue is not compulsion. It is the willing love of what is right. Where there is no choice, there is no virtue — only machinery.
translator_notes: Rhetorical Latin Christian — allow cadence without Victorian foam.

author: Arnobius
english: If souls are hurried along by fate and cannot turn aside, then the whole theater of courts and laws is a farce. Why punish what could never have been otherwise?
We hold that a person is answerable because a person can choose. Take that away, and praise and blame are empty noise.
translator_notes: Obscure to most Logos users; sharp pagan-world apologetic.

author: Minucius Felix
english: God is not honored by the blood of animals, but by a pure mind and a good conscience. The one who keeps innocence prays to God; the one who keeps justice makes offering to God.
We do not speak as those trapped by fate. We live as those who must give an account.

author: Commodian
english: There are two ways. One is of life; the other is of death. The difference between them is great. Choose life while the day of choosing remains.
translator_notes: Rough Latin poet — keep plain force, not polish into Victorian hymnody.

added_allusions.reason: Life and death set before you.

author: Hermas
english: First of all, believe that God is one, who created all things and set them in order, and made all things to come out of what was not into what is, and contains all things, and is himself alone uncontained.
Trust him, then, and fear him, and in fearing him practice self-control. Keep these things, and you will cast away all wickedness from yourself and put on every virtue of righteousness.
translator_notes: Popular in antiquity, sidelined in modern reading lists — include.

author: Hermas
english: The commandments are hard, you say, and no one can keep them. You must not say that. No one who has the Lord in his heart will find them hard.
Those who have the Lord on their lips but whose heart is hardened — to them the commandments are hard and difficult. Put the Lord in your heart, and you will find that nothing is easier.

author: Didache
english: There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways.
This is the way of life: first, you shall love the God who made you; second, you shall love your neighbor as yourself. Whatever you do not want to happen to you, do not do to another.

author: Barnabas
english: This is the way of light: if anyone wants to travel through to the appointed place, let him be eager in his works. The knowledge given to us for walking in it is of this sort: you shall love the One who made you; you shall fear the One who formed you; you shall glorify the One who redeemed you from death.

author: Barnabas
english: For this reason the Lord endured giving over his flesh to corruption: that we might be cleansed by the forgiveness of sins, that is, by the sprinkled blood of his death.

author: Ignatius of Antioch
english: Break one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying, so that we may live in Jesus Christ forever.
translator_notes: Ignatian intensity — short, piled, almost liturgical.

author: Ignatius of Antioch
english: Let no one be deceived. Even the heavenly beings and the glory of the angels, and the rulers visible and invisible — if they do not believe in the blood of Christ — judgment waits for them as well. The one who receives this is the one who has a place. The place is faith; love is the way.

author: Mathetes (Epistle to Diognetus)
english: When our unrighteousness was full, and it had been clearly shown that wages of punishment and death were expected, then the season came which God had appointed to reveal his own goodness and power.

O the surpassing kindness and love of God! He did not hate us, or reject us, or hold a grudge. He was patient; he bore with us. In pity he took up our sins. He gave his own Son as a ransom for us — the holy for the lawless, the innocent for the wicked, the just for the unjust, the incorruptible for the corruptible, the immortal for the mortal.
translator_notes: Often anonymous / lesser-assigned; luminous soteriology — keep the rising cadence.

author: Melito of Sardis
english: He was present in the slain lamb, and he was murdered in the lamb. He was led to slaughter in Abel, bound in Isaac, exiled in Joseph, sold in the price of silver.
He is the Passover of our salvation. He is the one who in many took many forms — and in the end was raised and cried aloud: Who contends against me? Let him stand before me.
translator_notes: Homiletic poetry — preserve parallelism; PD English thin on New Advent; expand from fuller PD/critical text later.

author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
english: There is one Lord, one of one, God of God, the stamp and image of the Godhead, the living Word, the true Wisdom, the true Light, the Life, the true Son — and through him we are saved.
translator_notes: Lesser-known Cappadocian forerunner; include for breadth of salvation language.

citation: Dionysius of Alexandria — On Nature (excerpt via Eusebius tradition)
author: Dionysius of Alexandria
english: Evil is not a substance God planted in the world. It is the turning of a free creature from what is fitting. Where the will goes crooked, corruption follows.
translator_notes: Fragmentary transmission — marked uncertain; keep until Greek fragment audit.

citation: Victorinus of Pettau — On the Creation of the World (excerpt)
author: Victorinus of Pettau
work: On the Creation of the World
english: Humanity was made in the image of God so that the one who rules the earth might himself be ruled by righteousness. The image is not a statue’s shape alone; it is the capacity to know and to choose.
translator_notes: Obscure Latin exegete — include.

author: Irenaeus
english: If it were not in our power to do these things or not to do them, what reason would the apostle have — and much more the Lord himself — to give us counsel to do some things and to abstain from others?
Because man has free will from the beginning, and God has free will, in whose likeness man was made, counsel is always given to keep hold of the good. That keeping happens through obedience to God.

author: Justin Martyr
english: The holy prophetic Spirit teaches us these things. We know that the demons have been defeated. Yet human beings still choose to serve what is worse. Prophecy names what will be; it does not chain the chooser.
translator_notes: Compressed; expand on full Greek/ANF pass for Second Apology fate discussion.

author: Tatian
english: We do not speak of fate. You who practice astrology invent a slavery of the sky. We say a person dies through personal fault, and lives again through personal willingness when God gives life.

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: The tree of knowledge was not evil as a tree. Disobedience was evil. The fruit was not death-dealing by nature; the transgression brought death.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The Lord of all draws near as a teacher. He does not drag the unwilling by the hair. He persuades. Those who can learn, learn; those who refuse remain responsible for the refusal.

author: Origen
english: This also is defined in the teaching of the church: that every rational soul has free will and choice; and that it has a struggle against the devil and his angels and opposing powers — because they strive to weigh the soul down with sins, while we, if we live rightly, try to be freed from them.

author: Lactantius
english: God wants us to be good. He does not force us. For what is forced is not virtue. He sets rewards before the willing and punishments before the stubborn, so that the will may be stirred by hope and by fear.

author: Methodius of Olympus
english: God’s foreknowledge does not impose necessity on what is foreknown. He sees what free creatures will do; he does not make them do it by seeing it. The eye that watches a runner does not push him down the track.
translator_notes: Sense-preserving modernization of Methodius’s anti-fatalist line.

author: Hermas
english: Luxury and deceit look like joy for a short time. Then they show what they are. The angel of punishment is not fate; he is the consequence that follows a life that would not turn.
translator_notes: Compressed from longer similitude; expand on next fidelity pass.

author: Mathetes (Epistle to Diognetus)
english: Christians are not distinguished from other people by land, language, or custom. They live in their own countries as sojourners. They marry as all do; they have children — but they do not discard them.
They live on earth, but their citizenship is in heaven. They obey the appointed laws, and by their own lives they surpass the laws.
translator_notes: Lived obedience as public apologetic — keep the poised paradoxes.
